steps.prompt: I think of a number, double it and add $7$. I get the same as when I triple it and take away $5$. What is my number? Can you write it as one equation?

cards.title: Name it, write it, solve it
cards.body: Give the unknown a letter and say what it stands for: "let $x$ be the number". Write what the words say, one phrase at a time. Then do the same thing to both sides until $x$ is alone. If there are fractions, multiply both sides by a common denominator first to clear them.

steps.text: Multiply both sides by $12$, which both $3$ and $4$ go into: $4x + 3x = 168$.

cards.title: Words into symbols
cards.body: "$5$ less than $x$" is $x - 5$, but "$x$ less than $5$" is $5 - x$. "Is" means $=$. Three consecutive whole numbers are $n$, $n + 1$, $n + 2$; consecutive odd (or even) numbers are $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$. Choosing the MIDDLE one as $n$ often makes the algebra shorter.

cards.title: Worked example: consecutive odd numbers
cards.problem: Three consecutive odd numbers add up to $117$. What is the largest?

steps.text: Call them $n$, $n + 2$ and $n + 4$. Their sum is $3n + 6 = 117$.
The numbers are $37$, $39$ and $41$. The question asks for the largest: $41$.

cards.title: The common trap: solving for the wrong thing
cards.body: Finding $n$ is not always the end: the question may ask for the largest number, or for $2n + 1$. Read the last line again before you answer. And watch the signs when you open brackets: $-(x - 3) = -x + 3$, and $-3(x - 1) = -3x + 3$.

prompts: Which phrase is easiest to turn into symbols the wrong way round? Write it both ways.
